title: Police conduct to be reviewed at inquests
article: One man was shot to death by city officers, and two other Winnipeggers died after being subdued by police.
The fourth inquest will examine the death of an elderly Laurier woman in a fire deliberately set at her care home.

Donald Lorne Miles, 34, was fatally shot by two city officers Nov. 5, 2001, at a gas station near Mountain Avenue and Salter Street. Miles, who had a record for assaulting a police officer and other offences and who was wanted for parole violation, allegedly lunged at police with a knife. Police said attempts to subdue Miles with pepper spray failed.
Shortly after the shooting, the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs called for an independent investigation into Miles? death.

Arthur Randy Gill, 45, died at the Health Sciences Centre last Feb. 10 after he became unresponsive while members of the Winnipeg Police Service were attempting to subdue him and place him in an ambulance.

Prior to his arrest, Gill was behaving in a bizarre fashion and had hurled himself through the plate glass window of a shop on Arlington Street. An autopsy confirmed he died as a result of agitated delirium due to cocaine use, a statement yesterday from chief medical examiner Dr. A. Thambirajah Balachandra?s office said.

Two witnesses criticized police at the time, saying they did little to aid Gill. But a police spokesman said the officers acted appropriately in attempting to subdue the man, and that ?the entire event from start to finish was captured on video?? from a nearby surveillance camera.
Laura Lee Draper, 39, died at St. Boniface General Hospital last Feb. 24 after suffering a cardiac arrest while being subdued by Winnipeg police officers.

The medical examiner?s office said the evening before, Draper apparently ran from her residence into the street without a coat, and was behaving in an agitated, disorderly manner. She was allowed into a nearby residence after telling the homeowners that someone was trying to kill her.

Police were called, and when they arrived Draper, due to her behaviour, was being restrained by the homeowners. She was subsequently apprehended by police, but went into cardiac arrest before the ambulance arrived. Despite resuscitation efforts, Draper sustained anoxic brain injury and was declared brain dead, the medical examiner?s office said. An autopsy showed she died as a result of cocaine use.

The Fatality Inquiries Act states that an inquest is mandatory when there is reasonable grounds to believe \`\`that a person died as a result of an act or omission of a peace officer in the course of duty.??
The Crown Attorney?s office will set dates for the inquests.

The chief medical examiner has also called an inquest into the death of Isobel Lathan, 76, of Laurier, on July 29, 2001, as a result of extensive burns she sustained in a fire at St. Christopher's House, the residential care home in which she lived. The manner of her death was ruled undetermined.

The Fire Commissioner's Office concluded the fire was deliberately set. Gerald Joseph Currie, 39, who was travelling by bus to Nova Scotia and was temporarily lodged at St. Christopher's House on the night of July 28, 2001, was charged. Last May, Currie pleaded guilty to criminal negligence causing death and was sentenced to 18 months.

The inquest has been called to determine the circumstances under which Lathan's death occurred, the availability and adequacy of mental health services to assess acutely psychotic patients in a rural setting in Manitoba, and to determine what, if anything, can be done to prevent similar deaths.
The Crown Attorney?s office in Dauphin will set the inquest date.
